title: Taylor and Maclaurin Series
trouble: Students forget the n! in the denominator.

blocks.html: Not every function is a geometric series in disguise. Taylor series give a recipe for any function you can differentiate again and again: the coefficients come from its higher derivatives at the center, using term-by-term differentiation.

Suppose $$\begin{aligned} f(x) = c_0 &+ c_1(x - a) + c_2(x - a)^{2} \\ &+ c_3(x - a)^{3} + \cdots. \end{aligned}$$ At $x = a$ every term but the first vanishes, so $c_0 = f(a)$. Differentiate once: $$\begin{aligned} f'(x) = c_1 &+ 2c_2(x - a) \\ &+ 3c_3(x - a)^{2} + \cdots, \end{aligned}$$ so $c_1 = f'(a)$. Again: $f''(x) = 2c_2 + 3\cdot 2\,c_3(x - a) + \cdots$, so $c_2 = \frac{f''(a)}{2}$. After $n$ differentiations the term $c_n(x - a)^{n}$ has become $n!\,c_n$, so
$$c_n = \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}.$$

The Taylor series of $f$ at $a$ is $\sum_{\role{index}{n}=0}^{\infty}\role[coefficient from the nth derivative]{coefficient}{\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}}\role[distance from the center a]{input}{(x - a)}^{n}$; at $a = 0$ it is called a Maclaurin series. The partial sum $T_n(x)$ is the Taylor polynomial of degree $n$: the polynomial that matches $f$ and its first $n$ derivatives at $a$.

blocks.title: The exponential
steps: The ratio test gives $R = \infty$, and (see the next topic) the series equals $e^{x}$ for every $x$.

blocks.html: Forgetting the $n!$. Writing $e^{x} \approx 1 + x + x^{2} + x^{3}$ uses $f^{(n)}(0)$ as the coefficient. At $x = 1$ that gives 4 instead of about $2.67$ (and $e \approx 2.718$). The factorial undoes the $n!$ that appears when you differentiate $(x - a)^{n}$ $n$ times. Check by differentiating your polynomial at the center: you should get back $f^{(n)}(a)$.

blocks.title: Sine
blocks.q: Find the Maclaurin series of $\sin x$.
steps: Only odd powers survive, with alternating signs: $$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= x - \frac{x^{3}}{3!} + \frac{x^{5}}{5!} - \cdots \\ &= \sum\frac{(-1)^{n}x^{2n+1}}{(2n + 1)!}. \end{aligned}$$
